passages.text: How do tornadoes form? There are thousands of thunderstorms in the United States each year, but only a few become strong enough to spin up a tornado. Few weather phenomena capture the imagination—or instill fear—like tornadoes. These swirling columns of wind can level entire communities in minutes, yet much about their formation remains shrouded in mystery. Still, scientists have uncovered key clues about how these powerful forces emerge from severe thunderstorms. Tornadoes don’t just appear out of nowhere. They need the perfect storm to form. It starts when warm, humid air clashes with cold air, which can generate a powerful thunderstorm known as a supercell. Although this can happen in many different parts of the world, it happens most often in the Plains, Midwest and Southeast regions of the United States, where the flat landscape across the center of North America allows cold air from the Arctic to dive south into the moisture-rich air from the Gulf. Thousands of thunderstorms form this way during the spring and summer, but only a few produce tornadoes. That's because one other ingredient is needed: wind shear. This happens in the same way that figure skaters spin faster when their arms are drawn in rather than when their arms are outstretched. This is called conservation of angular momentum. The rotating air moves horizontally across the ground, and can be tilted vertically by the force of the rising, rotating air. This allows a tornado to form. Most tornadoes form during supercell thunderstorms, but not all supercell thunderstorms produce tornadoes. Usually, the rotating air near the ground doesn't rotate fast enough for a tornado to form. If the rotating air near the ground is very cold, it will spread away from the storm along the ground and slow down like a figure skater with extended arms, and a tornado will not form.

Wind shear, which is when winds move at different speeds and directions in different parts of the atmosphere, is present in only the most severe thunderstorms. This often creates a horizontal spin in the air. The leading research on tornado formation says that the horizontal vortex of air turns vertical inside a severe thunderstorm with updrafts and downdrafts helping to create a mesocyclone, the rotating parent cloud of a tornado. A study published in 2018 found that tornadoes form from the ground up to the mesocyclone, contrary to popular thought. While most tornadoes form within powerful thunderstorms and follow the classic mesocyclone model, they’re not the only swirling threats out there. From landspouts to waterspouts and gustnadoes, more than a dozen other types of atmospheric vortexes exist—each with their own unique origins and behaviors. passages.text: Tornadoes form when powerful thunderstorms develop rotating air that becomes concentrated into a narrow, rapidly spinning column extending toward the ground. They most often occur when warm, moist air near the surface meets cooler, drier air above it, creating an unstable atmosphere. Strong changes in wind speed and direction with height can then help a thunderstorm develop rotation, while rising air currents may stretch that rotation and intensify it. When a rotating column of air extends from the storm to the ground, a tornado has formed. Although tornadoes are often associated with dramatic funnel clouds and violent winds, their development involves several distinct processes. Atmospheric instability supplies energy to thunderstorms, wind shear helps organize their rotation, and powerful updrafts reshape that rotation within the storm. Understanding how these factors interact explains why some thunderstorms produce tornadoes while many others do not. The atmospheric conditions that favor tornadoes Tornado-producing thunderstorms usually develop when the atmosphere contains a combination of moisture, instability, and wind shear. None of these ingredients guarantees a tornado on its own. Their interaction creates an environment in which a storm can grow strong, become organized, and sometimes develop a concentrated rotating circulation. Moisture often enters the lower atmosphere

What I tell kids Scientists are still studying exactly how tornadoes form. Although some of the details of tornado formation are still being investigated by scientists, we know the ingredients for tornadoes in a broad sense. In general, thunderstorms occur when warm, humid air near the ground is overlaid by relatively cold air aloft (in other words, temperatures cool rapidly with height). This variation of temperature with altitude results in what meteorologists refer to as “instability,” which gives energy to thunderstorms. Tornadoes can form within thunderstorms when instability is accompanied by what meteorologists refer to as “wind shear”—large changes in wind speed or direction with altitude. A tornado can also lift dust, soil, and debris into its rotating winds. This material can make the circulation visible below the cloud base, sometimes forming a debris cloud around the tornado’s lower portion. The debris cloud may be particularly important for identifying a tornado when condensation does not form a continuous funnel. The absence of a visible funnel does not prove that a tornado is absent. Likewise, a funnel-shaped cloud does not by itself establish that a tornado is in contact with the ground. Meteorologists consider radar data, storm structure, visual observations, and evidence of ground-level circulation when assessing tornado development. Thirty-second explanation of how tornadoes form in supercell thunderstorms (applicable to virtually all tornado outbreaks) Thunderstorms occur when warm, humid air near the surface lies beneath a deep layer of air in which the temperature decreases rapidly with height. Such an atmosphere is said to be “unstable,” which simply means that it contains ample energy to fuel thunderstorm updrafts. When an unstable atmosphere also is characterized by unusually high humidity near the surface and large changes in wind with height (“wind shear”), especially when considerable variation in wind is found over just the lowest few thousand feet of the atmosphere, tornado-producing supercell storms are possible. The science of tornadoes continues to advance through improved radar observations, numerical weather models, field measurements, and research into storm dynamics. A central goal is to understand how broad atmospheric conditions become concentrated into a dangerous circulation near the ground. Tornadoes emerge from the interaction of several physical processes rather than from a single cause. Warm, moist air and atmospheric instability help fuel thunderstorms, wind shear provides the potential for rotation, and the storm’s updraft and near-ground airflow can concentrate that rotation into a tornado. The combination explains both the power of these storms and why only a fraction of thunderstorms produce them.

Pressure differences, three-dimensional airflow, friction near the ground, and the storm’s evolving temperature structure all influence the circulation. A tornado forms when a sufficiently intense, organized rotating column of air becomes connected to the ground. The visible funnel cloud may appear during this development, but the cloud itself is not what creates the tornado. It forms when pressure and temperature changes cause water vapor to condense within the rotating air. Sometimes the near-ground circulation begins before a fully visible funnel develops. In other cases, a funnel cloud becomes visible before the circulation has clearly established contact with the surface. This is why visual appearance alone can be an imperfect guide to the precise stage of tornado formation. Why pressure drops and winds accelerate Tornadoes are associated with intense pressure differences and rapidly moving air. Within a rotating storm circulation, pressure often decreases toward the center, helping draw air inward. As air moves toward the circulation and rises, the combination of pressure forces and rotational dynamics can contribute to increasing wind speeds. It refers to a change in wind speed, wind direction, or both over a relatively short vertical distance. For example, winds near the ground might blow from the southeast while stronger winds several thousand feet above blow from the southwest. These differences can create a horizontal, rolling motion in the atmosphere that a thunderstorm may tilt and reorganize into vertical rotation. The most favorable tornado environments bring these ingredients together in the right proportions. A very unstable atmosphere can support vigorous thunderstorms, but without sufficient wind shear, those storms may lack sustained rotation. Strong wind shear alone is not enough if the atmosphere cannot support substantial upward motion. Even when both are present, tornado formation depends on smaller-scale processes within the storm that remain difficult to predict precisely. The central forecasting challenge is that tornado formation depends on processes occurring within an already complex storm. Two thunderstorms exposed to similar large-scale conditions may evolve differently because of subtle differences in their inflow, downdrafts, boundaries, and low-level circulations. These differences can determine whether a storm produces a tornado, how long it lasts, and how intense it becomes. Forecasting a favorable environment is therefore different from predicting the exact formation of a tornado at a particular location and time. Forecasters can issue watches when conditions favor tornado development and warnings when observations indicate an imminent or ongoing threat. Even with advanced instruments and improved understanding, uncertainty remains because the atmosphere is constantly changing and the decisive processes can occur on small spatial and temporal scales. The visible funnel can shrink or disappear as condensation changes, but a fading cloud does not necessarily indicate that all strong winds have stopped immediately. The actual wind circulation and the visible condensation cloud are related but distinct features. Some tornadoes weaken gradually, while others dissipate relatively quickly. A supercell may continue producing severe weather after a tornado ends, and it may sometimes produce another tornado if favorable conditions return. Tornado dissipation therefore marks the end of a particular ground-level circulation, not necessarily the end of the thunderstorm’s severe-weather threat. passages.text: How Tornadoes Form Tornadoes only form when a thunderstorm has a particular combination of winds. Air rising in a thunderstorm can begin to spin when it is affected by winds blowing it in different directions. It starts to rise and is pushed to the side by wind. It rises a bit more and is jostled again by wind moving in another direction. Winds moving in different speeds and directions at different altitudes cause the rising air to start spinning. Air that spins as it rises is typical in a supercell, the strongest type of thunderstorm, but not all spinning air creates a tornado. For a tornado to form, there also needs to be spinning air near the ground. This happens when air in the storm sinks to the ground and spreads out across it in gusts. Gusts of warmer air rise and gusts of cooler air sink as they blow across the land. If there are enough rising and sinking gusts, the air near the ground starts spinning. Wind shear creates the rotating updraft of supercell thunderstorms. Rotation next to the ground actually originates within a cool, descending airstream, however. Tornadoes form if the rotation within this cool air stream is greatly intensified. The intensification of the rotation occurs when the cool, rotating air is sucked upward into the overlying updraft of the supercell. The upward sucking is accompanied by an inward contraction of angular momentum, which increases the rotation in the same manner by which a figure skater spins faster. Photo by Bill Reid.

The vast majority of headline-making tornadoes are spawned by supercell thunderstorms, which are storms that are characterized by an updraft that rotates (counterclockwise rotation, if viewed from above, is most often observed, though some supercell updrafts rotate clockwise). Changes in wind speed and direction with altitude in the storm’s environment imply the presence of horizontal spin, similar to that of a football. As this spinning air is drawn into the storm’s updraft, the updraft rotates. Tornado formation is associated with a separate air stream, one that descends through a precipitation-driven downdraft and acquires horizontal spin by way of a horizontal variation of temperature along this air stream. If the air within this downdraft air stream is not too cold, this spinning air subsequently can be sucked upward by the supercell’s updraft, leading to a tornado. Our present understanding of how a tornado develops in a supercell thunderstorm.
